data.title: We Think Pioneer Power Solutions (NASDAQ:PPSI) Needs To Drive Business Growth Carefully
data.description:
We can readily understand why investors are attracted to unprofitable companies. For example, although Amazon.com made losses for many years after listing, if you had bought and held the shares since 1999, you would have made a fortune. But while history lauds those rare successes, those that fail are often forgotten; who remembers Pets.com?

So should Pioneer Power Solutions (NASDAQ:PPSI) shareholders be worried about its cash burn? For the purpose of this article, we'll define cash burn as the amount of cash the company is spending each year to fund its growth (also called its negative free cash flow). We'll start by comparing its cash burn with its cash reserves in order to calculate its cash runway.

This technology could replace computers: discover the 20 stocks are working to make quantum computing a reality.

When Might Pioneer Power Solutions Run Out Of Money?

A cash runway is defined as the length of time it would take a company to run out of money if it kept spending at its current rate of cash burn. As at September 2026, Pioneer Power Solutions had cash of US$9.4m and no debt. Importantly, its cash burn was US$8.1m over the trailing twelve months. data.title: What Investors Got Wrong About Applied Digital Before The Drop
data.description:
A year that featured Applied Digital signing a 15-year AI lease that pushed contracted revenue above US$23b, spinning off ChronoScale, and lining up huge power deals sounds like the kind of story long term holders hope for. Holding Applied Digital over the past year would have meant a 45.5% loss, including dividends. If you had bought on 20 November 2025, how much of that outcome was already hinted at in the early bull and bear cases?

A Narrative on Simply Wall St is one investor's written case for a company, with its growth, margin and multiple assumptions spelled out. Those assumptions imply an estimated Fair Value.

Applied Digital is not the only name tied to this theme. Zero in on 53 AI infrastructure stocks and compare how each one is priced.

The Two Applied Digital Stories Investors Had To Weigh

The shares cost US$21.37 at the start, and anyone looking at Applied Digital then was really choosing between two tight but very different stories.

The bullish narrative saw Fair Value at US$24, or 12% above the start price. That view leaned on assumed revenue growth of 82.0% a year over three years and profit margins shifting from heavy losses to 28.7%, supported by long AI leases.

The bearish case put Fair Value at US$13, or 39% below the start price. It accepted fast 75.4% revenue growth assumptions but focused on high debt and the risk that tighter regulation and supply chain problems would squeeze margins to just 2.6% and justify a 273.2x future P/E.

What The Evidence Did To The Applied Digital Story

Applied Digital signed several 15 year AI leases worth tens of billions of US dollars in contracted revenue, which directly backed the bullish focus on long contracts and hyperscaler demand. The measured results told a different story on profitability. Revenue reached US$341.9m in Q1 2027, while the business still reported a loss and net margin fell to -64.7%. The period cut both ways.

The whole episode turned on one assumption. You can accept aggressive growth forecasts only if you also track whether profit and net margin are actually moving toward the promised target, quarter by quarter, not just whether big contracts are announced.

What You Are Paying For In Applied Digital Today

Applied Digital trades at US$11.49 today after a 45.5% loss over the past year, and the bearish analyst Narrative on Simply Wall St places its Fair Value above that level based on contracted AI and HPC growth.

The same Narrative argues that for the higher figure to hold, new AI and power projects would need funding on terms that keep interest costs from overwhelming future earnings.

"Although Applied Digital highlights roughly $36 billion of contracted revenue across long term leases, the recent net loss of about $221 million from continuing operations in fiscal Q1 2027, driven by very high SG&A and noncash warrant losses, signals that scaling into this contract base could still leave the company struggling to translate future revenue into sustained earnings and cash flow."

That disagreement has a full argument behind it. → Uncover the higher Fair Value this Narrative argues for

Where Applied Digital’s Theme Extends

Applied Digital leans on huge AI workloads. Those workloads still need somewhere to run.

One large software and cloud provider is racing to host more of that demand. It sells access through subscriptions and usage based services.

The same customers pushing AI at Applied Digital often want integrated tools. This other business bundles office software, developer tools and agents around its cloud.

As AI projects expand, your question becomes sharper. Does value sit mostly in specialized infrastructure, or in platforms that tie AI, data and everyday software together?
